title: Extensions and Database-Side Capabilities
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose and key terms of extensions and database-side capabilities.
Apply database extension concepts in a small PostgreSQL-oriented example or design decision.
Validate the result against the expected behavior and identify one portability, safety, or edge-case consideration.

content.intro: Learn extensions and database-side capabilities through a short explanation, a concept diagram, and a PostgreSQL-oriented example. Focus on the reason for the query or design decision before memorizing syntax.
content.why_it_matters: Extensions and Database-Side Capabilities matters because database behavior becomes more reliable when the intended row meaning, data shape, and edge cases are explicit. This lesson follows the SQL curriculum's listed subtopics and calls out PostgreSQL-specific behavior when it matters.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Use extensions and database-side capabilities when database-side logic is justified by a clear contract. Document side effects, error behavior, transaction interactions, and engine-specific syntax; avoid hiding critical business behavior in surprising triggers.

content_blocks.title: Apply the idea
content_blocks.text: Start with the subtopics: Database extension concepts, Installing or enabling supported extensions, Custom functions and operators, Extension permission requirements. Define the result you expect, run or inspect the small example in your own disposable PostgreSQL lab, and change one assumption at a time. The embedded lesson editor is a demonstration shell: the current project shows the sample expected output and does not execute arbitrary SQL on the server.

items.title: Database extension concepts
items.text: Database extension concepts helps you recognize procedural SQL dialects and design server-side functions, procedures, triggers, error handling, and dynamic SQL deliberately. Start with a concrete example, state the expected result, and verify the behavior before extending the query or design.

items.title: Installing or enabling supported extensions
items.text: Installing or enabling supported extensions is part of a repeatable development workflow. Use a dedicated local lab, check the connection target before running changes, save scripts in version control, and keep credentials out of source files.

items.title: Custom functions and operators
items.text: Custom functions and operators works best when inputs and outputs have deliberate types. Use explicit casts when intent is unclear, guard against overflow or truncation, and avoid converting typed values to display strings before calculations finish.

items.title: Extension permission requirements
items.text: Extension permission requirements should be enforced at the database/application boundary rather than by UI checks alone. Bind data values as parameters, grant only the access a role needs, and test that unauthorized operations fail.

content_blocks.code: SELECT name, default_version, installed_version FROM pg_available_extensions WHERE name IN ('pg_trgm', 'pgcrypto', 'postgis') ORDER BY name;

content_blocks.reset_steps: For queries, restore the original text and compare results. For statements that change data, use the transaction and rollback shown in the example, or recreate the disposable lab from the included setup instructions. Do not reset production data.

content_blocks.title: Remember
content_blocks.text: SQL correctness depends on data shape, constraints, NULL behavior, row counts, and the target database dialect—not just whether a statement parses.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming a query is correct because it returns some rows.
common_mistakes.why: A result can omit valid records, multiply joined rows, mishandle NULLs, or rely on a non-deterministic order.
common_mistakes.fix: Check the expected row grain, add targeted edge cases, and use a stable tie-breaker whenever order or pagination matters.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying PostgreSQL syntax into another SQL engine without checking support.
common_mistakes.why: PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite, SQL Server, and Oracle differ in types, functions, row limits, procedural features, and transaction behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: Label the target engine/version and verify the relevant official reference before adapting the query.

common_mistakes.problem: Testing with production data or credentials.
common_mistakes.why: Practice statements can change rows or expose sensitive information if run against the wrong connection.
common_mistakes.fix: Use a dedicated disposable lab, check current_database() and current_user, and review all changes before committing.
